newsitem.title: YEMEN: Aden hoping to return as major port.
newsitem.headline: Aden hoping to return as major port.

text.p: Yemeni officials said on Monday they expected dredging in Aden harbour to start on April 17 under a project to restore the port as a key staging post between Europe and Asia.
It would be the first tangible work to revive the port, an important element of the Aden Free Zone, a $500 million project to make Yemen's economic and commercial capital a major trans-shipment hub.
The world's fourth largest dredger arrived over the weekend from Singapore on a 15 week mission to scoop out enough sand to accommodate the world's largest container vessels.
The removed sand will be used to create an island to host a new port and a container station opposite the existing port of Aden, the officials said.
It will have six quays and a 16 metre (52 feet)-deep navigational channel, increased from 12 metres, with all services and facilities.
"Dredging will be a major part needed to allow us to complete all construction for the first phase of the project," said Dirham Abdo Noman, Aden Free Zone chief.
"The Aden Free Zone area will become a reality now after it was a long-awaited dream," he told a ceremony ahead of the dredging operations.

The Aden project is being driven by the Yemeni Investment and Development Company (YEMINCO), an international consortium which includes Saudi investors of Yemani origin, as well as Saudi and U.S. development firms. Meneren Corporation of the United States is in charge.
Ahmed Saleh bin Farid, YEMINCO's chief executive officer said dredging and other operations would end by July while the piers and cargo station would be ready by March 1999 at a cost of $250 million.
Aden aims to offer facilities and fast turnaround for the largest carriers now plying routes from Europe through the Suez Canal and the Red Sea to Southeast Asia, Australia and East Africa.
Aden's revival is a challenge to regional rivals -- Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Jeddah and the Gulf ports of Dubai and Jebel Ali in the United Arab Emirates, which are shallower.

Aden was once an important staging post for shipping between Europe, the Mediterranean and Asia. Some 7,000 vessels called each year during the 1950s and 1960s but war and political uncertainty drove trade elsewhere.
